beats.narration_text: Hallo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Episode four of five: run the prompt, then turn an adversarial move against it. Two components, twenty-two points total. What separates them from the earlier deliverables is evidence. A specification can be written in the abstract. A worked example requires you to actually run the prompt and show the output. An adversarial self-critique requires you to actually run the attack and show a revision it drove. 'I ran it' without the output is not a worked example. 'I applied a steelman' without the revision is not an adversarial critique. The quartile bonus rewards precisely this — real work leaves traces that described work does not.

props.command: Run your adapted prompt. Show the output. Write analytical commentary. Then pick an adversarial move, run it against your own prompt, and produce the revision.

beats.act: the worked example — what it requires
beats.narration_text: The worked example has three parts. First: run the adapted prompt on actual content from your domain. Not a constructed example, not a hypothetical — actual work. A real document, a real decision context, a real input the model would see in professional use. Second: include the output. Full, or meaningfully excerpted — but the output must be there. A description of what the output contained is not the output. Third: write analytical commentary on what the output showed you. What worked — specifically. What failed — specifically. What you would change after seeing it, and why. And, critically: what a fluent practitioner in your domain would catch that you did or did not catch. That last question is where the domain knowledge earns its points.

The commentary is where most worked examples lose points. Descriptive commentary is: 'The model produced a clear summary with the key points covered.' That tells the grader nothing about whether the summary was correct, whether it failed in ways the model could not detect, or whether you know your domain well enough to evaluate it. Analytical commentary is: 'The model correctly identified the Beers Criteria contraindication but failed to flag the dose-adjustment requirement for renal impairment — a standard clinical check that an attending would expect a pharmacist to surface. I added a renal function constraint to the Exclusions after seeing this.' That is two things: a named failure the model produced, and a change you made because you saw it. Analytical commentary changes something. Descriptive commentary describes something that already happened.

beats.narration_text: The adversarial self-critique gives you four moves. Steelman: construct the strongest version of an objection to your prompt's core assumption — if the steelman holds, the prompt needs to change. Edge-case probe: identify an input at the boundary of your prompt's intended use where the prompt would produce a harmful or misleading output — write that input, run it, see what happens. Assumption surface: list the premises your prompt is silently relying on — role knowledge, output use, reviewer behavior — and check whether any of them fail to hold. Devil's advocate: argue that the prompt's design produces a worse outcome than no prompt at all, and see if that argument finds purchase. Pick the move that most threatens your prompt's actual design. The move that finds nothing is the wrong move.

lines: Pick the one that most threatens your prompt's actual design
STEELMAN: Build the strongest objection to your prompt's core assumption
EDGE-CASE PROBE: Find an input at the boundary

beats.act: the move must produce a substantive revision
beats.narration_text: The adversarial move must produce a revision that is substantive — not cosmetic. A cosmetic revision changes a word or reorders a sentence. A substantive revision changes what the prompt asks for, what it excludes, what it permits, or what the success criteria are. The test: if you removed the adversarial move from your submission, would the revision still make sense? If yes, the revision was cosmetic — it did not actually follow from the attack. A substantive revision is traceably caused by the move that produced it. Include both in your deliverable: the move, then the revision, then one sentence connecting them — here is what the attack found, and here is what changed because of it.

lines: The revision must be traceable to the attack
COSMETIC: changes a word, reorders a sentence
SUBSTANTIVE: changes what the prompt asks for, excludes, permits, or how

beats.narration_text: Three traps across these two components. First: describing the run without the output. 'I ran the prompt and got a helpful response' is not a worked example. The output must be present in the deliverable. Second: naming the adversarial move without running it. 'I applied an edge-case probe' followed by a paragraph about what an edge case probe is — not what it found — is a description of a move, not a move. Third: a cosmetic revision presented as substantive. Adding 'please be thorough' to the end of your prompt after an adversarial analysis is not a revision the attack drove. The grader knows the difference between a revision that follows from an attack and one that does not. So does the quartile score.

lines: All three show up in quartile-bottom submissions

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: 'I have an adapted Botspeak prompt. Here it is: [your adapted prompt from E3]. Run a steelman adversarial move against this prompt. First, construct the strongest objection to the prompt's core assumption — the thing the prompt is most relying on being true. Make the steelman as strong as you can. Then tell me: if the steelman holds, what specifically in the prompt needs to change — the intent, the constraints, the exclusions, the output format, or the success criteria — and draft the change. The revision should be traceable to the steelman.' Run this. If the model finds nothing threatening, you may have the wrong move — try the edge-case probe instead. The move that finds something is the one to use.
